plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line drawing of a graphical model laid out as a two-dimensional lattice in oblique projection, built from two kinds of nodes. Open white circles occupy the lattice sites, arranged in three receding rows of three visible sites each; within a row they are joined by horizontal edges that run past the rightmost circle to the frame edge, and between rows by short diagonal edges slanting down and to the left, which likewise continue off the lower-left corner, so the grid reads as a fragment of an unbounded array. A single vertical edge rises from each white circle to a solid gray filled circle, one gray node per site, drawn above and slightly behind its partner. Only the back row carries labels: its white circles are marked with the boldface symbols x_1, x_2, and x_3, and the gray circles directly above them y_1, y_2, and y_3. Because every gray node hangs off exactly one white node while the white nodes alone form the grid, the drawing separates per-site attachments from neighbor-to-neighbor coupling. The structure depicts a Markov random field over a spatial grid, each site carrying a state variable tied to its four lattice neighbors.

elements: 9 white open-circle nodes arranged in a 3x3 lattice (3 columns x 3 receding rows)
9 solid gray filled nodes, one suspended directly above each white node
horizontal black edges joining white nodes within each row, extending past the rightmost circle to the frame edge
diagonal black edges (receding depth direction) joining white nodes between adjacent rows, slanting down-left and continuing off the lower-left corner
vertical black edges rising from each white node to its gray node
boldface labels x1, x2, x3 on the three back-row white nodes
boldface labels y1, y2, y3 on the three back-row gray nodes

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Separates the two factor types of the MRF: the white-grid edges encode neighbor-to-neighbor pairwise coupling, while the vertical gray links encode per-site observation evidence; seeing them in isolation clarifies which edges carry which potential

Clicking a white x node isolates its Markov blanket — its four lattice neighbors plus its attached gray y node — while all other edges fade, making the local conditional-dependence structure x_i | neighbors, y_i visually explicit

interactions.label: Coupling strength
interactions.teaches: As pairwise coupling grows, each white node's shade relaxes toward the mean of its neighbors, so the field becomes spatially smooth; the gray observation nodes stay fixed, showing that smoothness is driven purely by the neighbor potentials, not the evidence

demo_steps.title: Full model
demo_steps.narration: Both edge families are drawn: the white grid (neighbor coupling) and the vertical gray links (per-site observations). This is the complete MRF factor graph.

demo_steps.title: Hidden lattice only
demo_steps.narration: Only the white-grid edges remain. These horizontal and diagonal links are the pairwise potentials that couple each site to its four lattice neighbors.

demo_steps.title: Observations only
demo_steps.narration: Only the vertical gray links remain. Each gray y node hangs off exactly one white x node, encoding the unary observation potential at that site.

demo_steps.title: Strong coupling
demo_steps.narration: With coupling near 1 the white nodes blend toward their neighbors' average shade and the field looks smooth, while the gray nodes keep their fixed color — smoothness comes from the pairwise term alone.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Oblique lattice in the X-Z plane with Y as the vertical attachment axis. Columns along +X at x = 0, 1.5, 3.0; rows recede along +Z (screen up-right) at z = 0, 1.5, 3.0; white nodes at y = 0, gray nodes at y = +1.2 directly above their partner. Node spheres radius ~0.18 world units. Horizontal edges run along +X within each row and extend ~1.5 past the last column; depth edges run along +Z between rows and extend ~1.5 toward the viewer (lower-left) past the front row, so the grid reads as a fragment of an unbounded array. Vertical edges connect (x,0,z) to (x,1.2,z). Colors: white nodes fill #ffffff stroke #000000; gray nodes fill #808080 stroke #000000; all edges #000000; labels #000000 bold. Coupling shading: give each white node a fixed base value b_i in [0,1]; displayed value v_i = lerp(b_i, mean(b over 4-neighbors), coupling); map v to a white->#3a7bd5 ramp. Gray nodes never change color. Labels x1,x2,x3 / y1,y2,y3 only on the back row (z = 3.0).
interactionPlan.notes: Three.js: SphereGeometry per node (white = MeshBasicMaterial white + a thin black outline via a slightly larger back-side sphere or EdgesGeometry; gray = #808080). Edges as LineSegments with transparent material so opacity can fade on selection. Raycast clicks against the 9 white spheres only; on select, set blanket edges/nodes opacity=1 and all others ~0.12. Toggle shows/hides the horizontal+diagonal edge group vs the vertical edge+gray-node group. Recompute white node colors reactively on every coupling slider change; keep gray colors constant. Use a fixed oblique pose so horizontal edges stay screen-horizontal and depth recedes up-right.

- Click any white x node to highlight its four neighboring x nodes and its attached gray y node; all other edges fade, making the local Markov blanket and conditional dependence structure visible.
- Toggle between hidden-state lattice, observation attachments, and full model views; white grid edges, gray vertical links, or both appear in turn, separating neighbor coupling from per-site evidence.

authoredContext:
To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a Markov random field (MRF):

Two-dimensional Markov random field.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in the figure, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (the figure [a]). The figure [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red. (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.

Replace the back-side outline spheres with a thinner single-stroke circle outline to match the source's fine line weight
